transcript.content: Right, let's get into it. Thinking about the places where you actually spend time with your male friends — what's your favourite spot in your area for that? Could be a pub, somewhere outdoors, someone's house, whatever comes to mind. And why that place?

Yeah, so for me it's probably the pub down the road, to be honest. It's just... convenient, innit. Close to where I live, doesn't take much to get there. The usual group goes there regularly, so you know you'll bump into someone most evenings if you fancy a pint. Plus the food's decent enough — not fancy or anything, but it does the job. And it's just relaxed, no pressure to stay long or anything. You can just show up, have a drink, a chat, and if someone wants to grab some food there's options. That's probably why we end up there more than anywhere else really.

Yeah, that makes sense. It's the same sort of thing for us really. There's a couple of pubs near where I am, and you just get into the habit of going to the same one, don't you. Everyone knows where you'll be, so if someone wants to meet up they just show up. It's not like you have to plan it all out.

And to your point about the food — yeah, it's not anything special, but that's kind of the thing. You're not going for a fancy meal or anything. It's just... there if you want it. A burger or whatever. In a smaller area like mine, you don't really have that many options anyway, so the pub just becomes the default spot. Easier than trying to go somewhere else, trying to organize people. This way it just happens naturally.

Yeah, exactly. And it's interesting because London's got loads of options, right — you've got restaurants, bars, all sorts — but we still just default to the same pub. I think it's almost the same logic though. Like, you know the place, you don't have to think about it, everyone else knows it too. There's a comfort in that. You're not spending half the evening deciding where to go or ringing people round trying to organize something fancy. You just go to the pub, job done. So even though we've got way more choice here, we're basically doing the same thing you lot are — taking the easy option.

But that's a bit different though, isn't it? I mean, you've got the choice to go somewhere else if you wanted. You're choosing the pub because it's easy and comfortable and everyone knows it. Fair enough. But for us, it's more... there's not really anywhere else to go. The pub's it. So it's not quite the same thing as choosing the default when you've got options.

Like, if I fancied trying somewhere different, I'd have to drive into Belfast or somewhere, which is a bit of a hassle. Whereas you could just say to your mates, right, fancy trying that new Italian place or whatever, and you're sorted. We don't really have that luxury. So yeah, we end up at the same pub, but it's more because there's nothing else than because we're choosing comfort over something better. That's just what's available to us.

Fair point, yeah. You're right — that's not quite the same thing. I mean, we could go somewhere different if we wanted to bother, but we just... don't. Whereas you're working with what's actually there. That's a different situation entirely. I wasn't really thinking about it like that. So it's less about choosing comfort and more about just, that's what you've got. Makes sense.

That's an interesting distinction — having options and not using them is a different thing from not having them at all. Sam, Henry, Bilal — what about where you are? Same kind of story, or does it look different?

Yeah, it's a bit like what Noah said really. I mean, we've got a couple of pubs locally, and that's sort of where we end up. There's maybe one or two other spots — a cafe, that kind of thing — but they're not really the same vibe, you know? Not somewhere you'd naturally take your mates for an evening.

I think the difference with where I am is it's suburban, so you're kind of in that middle ground. It's not London where you've got endless options on your doorstep, but it's not like Belfast where you'd have to drive somewhere to get variety. There are options if you really wanted to drive out and find them, but honestly... why would you? The pub's there, it's familiar, everyone knows it. So we just go there like Connor said. But I don't think we're conscious we're choosing comfort over something better, like. It's just what you do. It's where you go.

Though now that Noah mentions it, yeah — there's something different about having the choice available and not bothering versus just not having it in the first place. I suppose we're closer to Connor's situation than Noah's, but we're not really thinking about what we might be missing either. It just is what it is.
Henry, Bilal — what's it like where you are? Does that land the same way?

Yeah, I'd say it's more like Connor's situation actually. I mean, Birmingham's got loads going on — you've got restaurants, different bars, all that. But honestly, me and my mates, we just end up at the same couple of pubs we've always gone to. There's one in particular that's just become the default, you know? It's near where a few of us live, everyone knows it, the regulars know us. 

And like Connor said, you could go somewhere different if you fancied it, but you just... don't bother. There's no real reason to. The pub does food, the beer's fine, it's comfortable. You know what you're getting. So even though there's definitely other stuff around, we don't really use it. 

But I think what Noah's saying makes sense too — we're choosing not to bother, whereas if you've got nothing else nearby you're just getting on with what's there. Different thing. We could probably be more adventurous about it if we wanted, but we're not.
Bilal, what's it like in Leeds — similar sort of thing?

Yeah, it's pretty much like what Henry's saying, to be honest. Leeds has got loads of restaurants, bars, all that stuff — you can find anything really if you look. But me and my mates, we just... we've got our spots, haven't we. There's a couple of pubs we end up at most of the time. One in particular that's just become the thing.

And I think it's the same as what Connor and Henry are saying — we could go somewhere different if we wanted, but we just don't. It's easier not to. Everyone knows where you'll be, you don't have to think about it, the food's fine, whatever. So even though there's definitely other options around, we're not really using them.

I get what Noah's saying though — that's a different situation if you've literally got nothing else. But yeah, for me it's more... we're choosing the easy option when we could probably do something else if we bothered. Which I suppose we could think about more, but we just don't.

Sounds like whatever the city, the pull towards familiar spots is pretty strong — even when there's no shortage of alternatives. Let's shift gears a bit. Thinking about your day-to-day now — how do you actually decide what to eat? What goes into that for you?

I mean, honestly, it's not really that straightforward for me day-to-day. Like, yeah, we just said we go to the same pubs, but actually when it comes to what I'm eating... it's more random than that.

Some days I'll just grab something quick because I'm busy, yeah, but other times I'll think, right, I fancy trying that new place I heard about, and I'll go. Or it depends who I'm with — if I'm with certain mates we'll go somewhere specific, but if I'm on my own or with different people, I might do something else. 

I think I was a bit... I dunno, painting it like we're all just defaulting to the same thing every time, but that's not really how it works for me. Some weeks I'm trying places I've not been before. Other weeks I'm just grabbing whatever's nearest because I can't be bothered. It's just... depends on the day really, depends on what's going on, who I'm with.

So I don't know if I was being honest before or just going along with the pattern everyone was describing, but yeah, it's a bit messier than that.

Yeah, fair point that. I think I'm the same actually. When I said we just go to the same pubs, that's true for meeting up with mates, but day-to-day eating? It's definitely not that straightforward for me either.

Like, some weeks I'll be grabbing a Tesco meal deal at lunchtime because I'm at work and can't be bothered, other times I'll get a takeaway from somewhere different — depends what I'm in the mood for really. And weekends are different again. If I'm going out with the lads it's the pub, yeah, but if I'm just... I dunno, at home or doing something on my own, it's completely different.

I think I kind of nodded along with what everyone was saying because the pub thing is true, and it's easy to talk about, but actually my eating's all over the place when you think about it properly. Some nights I'll cook something, other nights I can't be arsed and just order something. Sometimes I'll deliberately try somewhere new because I've heard about it, sometimes I just want the same old thing because it's easy.

So I don't think I was being fully honest either, if I'm being honest. It's messier than just defaulting to one thing.

Yeah, that's what I mean, innit. It's weird — we all sort of... agreed on this thing about defaulting and choosing comfort, and it sounded right when we were saying it. But then you actually think about what you do and it's nothing like that simple.

I think it's because the pub thing is easy to explain, isn't it? It's a clear pattern. But actually living it, it's just loads of little decisions based on what's happening that day — how tired you are, who you're with, what you fancy, whether you've got time. Some days I'll genuinely want to try something new because I've heard about it or whatever. Other days I can't be bothered and just go for the same thing. Neither of those things is about choosing comfort over something better. It's just... that's what makes sense that day.

I think we just kind of... defaulted to the simple answer when everyone was agreeing on it. It felt like that was the point of the conversation, so we went with it. But the reality's just messier than that, like you said.

Right, yeah. And I think the thing is — the pub's not really about food at all, is it? That's what I'm realizing. We go there because that's where everyone goes, that's the routine, that's where your mates will be. The food's just... there. It happens to be available. But that's not a food choice in the way we're talking about day-to-day eating.

Like, when I'm at home trying to work out what to have for tea, or grabbing lunch at work, that's an actual choice. But going to the pub with the lads — that's not me choosing comfort over something better or being adventurous. It's just going where you go. The food's incidental to that, you know?

I think we've kind of mixed those two things up. We've been talking about them like they're the same decision, but they're not really. One's about the social thing, the routine with your mates. The other's about what you actually eat day-to-day. They're separate.

So yeah, I agree with Bilal — we kind of fell into explaining it in a simple way that made sense when everyone was nodding along, but when you break it down, the pub's not really about food choices at all. That's a different thing.

That distinction Henry's drawing — the pub being about the routine rather than the food — feels like a useful place to leave that thread. Let's take it somewhere related. Thinking about what you actually eat, not just where you go — do you think your gender influences what you eat? Why or why not?

I mean... yeah, I think it probably does, doesn't it. Not in like a big conscious way, but yeah.

Like, I wouldn't necessarily sit down and think about it, but if I'm honest, I probably go for certain things more than I would if I was a woman, or if I thought about it differently. Stuff that's seen as more... I dunno, "proper" food maybe? Meat-heavy stuff, burgers, that kind of thing. And I think that's partly because you don't really get the same... pressure around it, do you? Like, there's not the same expectation that you have to be thinking about what you're eating in a particular way.

And when I'm with my mates at the pub, that's definitely a thing. No one's ordering a salad, are they. You'd get ripped for it. So there's that social thing too — what's acceptable, what people expect you to be eating when you're in that group.

But day-to-day on my own? I'm not sure it changes that much. I eat what I fancy. Though I suppose even what I fancy is probably shaped by that stuff over time, if you know what I mean. It's just become normal.

I don't know if that's really what you're asking though. Is it more about... health stuff, or just like, what people choose?

Sam's making a distinction there that I think is worth the rest of you reacting to — between the social situation, where there's a real sense of what's expected, and then day-to-day on your own, where it might be less visible but still kind of there. Does that match what any of you experience, or does it land differently?

Yeah, no, that's exactly it for me. Sam's nailed that actually. 

Like, at the pub with the lads — yeah, there's definitely that thing where you're not going to order a salad or something light. You just wouldn't. Not because anyone's explicitly saying anything most of the time, but you know what's... acceptable, I guess. What fits. You'd get a burger, steak, something like that. Proper food. And if someone did order a salad, yeah, you'd get comments.

But what Sam said about day-to-day — I think that's where it gets interesting, because even when I'm on my own, I'm probably going for the same kind of stuff anyway. And I don't think it's just habit or whatever. I think it is shaped by all that social stuff over time, like he said. It becomes what you actually want because it's what you've always done, what's been normal. So it's not like I sit down thinking, right, I'm a man so I should eat this. It's just... that's what feels right to me.

And honestly, in a smaller area like mine where there's not much choice anyway, and everyone's going to the same couple of pubs anyway, that social pressure's probably stronger because you're all seeing the same people all the time, you know? It just becomes the norm pretty quickly.

Yeah, I get that. I think you're right about the social pressure being there even when you're on your own — it does kind of sink in over time. But I'm not sure it's necessarily stronger in smaller areas though, to be honest.

Like, I live in a suburban area, so I'm not London where there's endless choice and anonymity or whatever, but I'm also not as isolated as Noah where you're seeing the same people all the time. And I think what I've noticed is... it depends who you actually spend time with, doesn't it? Not just where you live.

I mean, yeah, if you're going to the same pub with the same group of lads every week, then yeah, that pressure builds. But I've got mates where that's the case, and I've got other people I see who are just completely different about it. Like, one of my mates will order whatever he wants, don't care. Another one will probably think about it more. It's not really about living in a smaller area — it's more about... the actual group you're in, I think.

So I don't know if I'd say the pressure's stronger in smaller places necessarily. It might just feel more obvious because there's fewer places and fewer people, so the patterns stand out more. But where I am, you can kind of... opt out of it if you want to, even though it's not a massive city. It just depends who you're spending time with, really.

Yeah, but that's the thing though — you can opt out because there are other people to spend time with, or other things to do. Like, if you wanted to avoid that group at the pub, you could go somewhere else, or hang out with different people, or just stay in. There's room to move around.

Where I am, it's not really like that. The pub is where everyone goes. That's your social life, basically. So you're not choosing to opt in or out of a particular group dynamic — you're just... in it, because that's where you go. There's not really an alternative.

I mean, yeah, fair enough, you get different personalities in any group. Someone might not care, someone might be more self-conscious about it. But the baseline is the same — everyone's working within the same few options, seeing the same people. So when Sam says no one orders a salad and you'd get ripped for it, that's not just his particular mate group. That's just... what happens. That's the culture of the place.

Whereas you could theoretically find a different crowd or a different spot where people are more relaxed about it. We could too, I suppose, but we'd have to drive to Belfast, and at that point you're not really hanging out locally anymore, are you? So it's a different thing.

Right, yeah, I hear what you're saying. And I think you're actually making a fair point about constraint versus just... not bothering to look. 

But I'm wondering if I'm kind of in the same boat as you without really thinking about it that way. Like, I said you can opt out, but can you, really? I mean, theoretically yeah, there are other pubs or bars or whatever in the area, but are there? I haven't actually... I don't know if I've properly looked, to be honest. I've just settled into the routine with my mates at the same place, and I've not really thought about whether there are actual alternatives or if I've just stopped looking because it's easier not to.

And you're right — when you put it like that, the difference between having a choice available and choosing not to bother versus just not having it at all gets a bit blurry for me. Because I don't actually know if I've got real alternatives. I just assume I do because I'm in a bigger area than you are. But I might just be doing the exact same thing — defaulting to what's there and not bothering to check if there's something different.

So I don't know. Maybe the suburban thing isn't the middle ground I was thinking it was. Maybe I'm just... not questioning it the same way you're being forced to question it because you genuinely don't have the options.

Sam's just questioned his own assumption there — whether the sense of having options is real or just assumed. Henry, Bilal, Connor — does any of that land for you? Do you recognise the thing they're describing, or does it feel different from where you're sitting?

Yeah, I think... I reckon I'm in the same boat as Sam actually. Like, I said earlier London's got loads of choice, but when you really think about it, do I actually use any of that? I go to the same pub with the same people, end up ordering the same kind of thing. And I never really question it because the options are there, so I assume I'm choosing. But I'm probably not choosing at all — I'm just doing the default thing like everyone else.

The difference is I could go somewhere different if I wanted to, right? But the point is I'm not bothering. And I think once you stop bothering, after a while you just... forget that you're choosing not to. It just becomes what you do. So yeah, in a way maybe it's not that different from what Noah's describing. I've got the options available, but I'm not using them any more than he is — I'm just not as aware of it because they exist.
Henry, you've been quiet on this one — does any of what they're describing match your experience, or does it feel different?

Yeah, I think I'm probably... I dunno, somewhere in that. Like Connor, I've got the options there in Birmingham. But honestly, I'm probably not using them either. I just go to the same places with the same people and that's it.

But I think what's interesting in what Sam and Connor are saying is — you don't really know if you're choosing not to bother or if you've just accepted it as the norm without thinking about it. Like, I couldn't tell you if there are other pubs or restaurants I'd actually enjoy because I'm not looking. I've just settled into this routine and I'm not questioning it.

So when we talk about what I eat and whether my gender influences it — yeah, it probably does. But I can't really separate that out from just... what I've always done, what's normal in my group. I eat meat-heavy stuff, burgers at the pub, whatever. But I don't know if that's because I'm a bloke or because that's just what's available where I go and what everyone around me does.

The thing about the salad comment though — yeah, you'd definitely get comments. And I think that does sink in over time, like Noah said. But I'm not sure I'm actively thinking about my gender when I order. It's just... what feels right because it's what you do.

I'm not sure I've really got a strong answer on whether gender influences what I eat, to be honest. It probably does, but it's all mixed up with the routine and the group and just... not bothering to think about it differently.

Henry, I want to pick up on something you said a bit earlier — back when you were talking about your day-to-day eating, you said it was 'all over the place' and that you hadn't been fully honest in how you'd described it before. But just now you're describing it as meat-heavy stuff, burgers at the pub, what everyone does. How do those two sit together for you?

Yeah, fair point. I think... when I said it was all over the place, I meant more — like, some days I'm grabbing a meal deal, some days I'm cooking something at home, some days it's a takeaway. That kind of thing. The variety in where and how I'm eating.

But when it comes to what type of food, like, the actual meat-heavy stuff — yeah, that's pretty consistent. I don't think I'm varying that much. It's more the context that changes, you know? The pub's one situation, but even when I'm on my own or at home, I'm still probably reaching for the same kind of thing. A burger, a steak, whatever.

So maybe "all over the place" was the wrong way to put it. It's more just... not always the pub. But the actual food choices are probably pretty narrow, now you mention it. I don't really go for lighter stuff or salads or whatever. That's just not what I eat.

And I suppose that's the thing we were talking about — that social pressure thing, how it becomes what you actually want over time. I'm probably eating that way because that's what's normal, what's expected. But I can't really separate that out from what I actually fancy anymore because it's all the same thing to me.

Yeah, that makes sense — it's the context that shifts, not what ends up on the plate. I think that's a useful distinction. Okay, let's move on because I want to make sure we get to something I'm keen to hear you all on. Imagine you actually decided to go plant-based — not just cut back a bit, but properly shift. What would need to change in your life for that to be realistic?

I mean... honestly, a lot would need to change. Like, the pub thing on its own — that's already hard because everyone's ordering burgers and that. If I went plant-based, that's a whole different dynamic, isn't it. You're the one person ordering something different, and yeah, you'd definitely get comments. That's real.

But more than that, practically... I'd need to actually know what to eat. Like, I don't cook much. Most of my eating is just grabbing something quick or ordering takeaway or going to the pub. I haven't got the knowledge or the routine around it to suddenly do plant-based. I'd have to learn what meals actually work, where to get them from, all that.

And honestly, time-wise, it would take more effort, wouldn't it? Finding places that do decent plant-based options when you're out, or cooking something at home instead of just grabbing whatever's easiest. That's the real thing for me — it's not like I'm choosing burgers because I think they're better or whatever. It's just... they're there, they're easy, they're what everyone does. Going plant-based would mean actually thinking about it every time I eat, and I'm not sure I've got the headspace for that.

So yeah, it wouldn't just be about the social side of it, though that's definitely part of it. It would be the actual... logistics of it. How I buy food, how I eat day-to-day, all of that would have to shift. And right now I can't really see what would make me do that.

Yeah, and I think what Bilal's saying about the logistics is real — you'd have to actually learn stuff, find places, all that. But I think there's something else in there too that he's kind of touching on but not quite saying.

Like, he said he'd have to think about it every time he eats. And I think that's the thing, isn't it? Right now, going to the pub and ordering a burger — you don't have to think about it. It's just what you do. It's automatic. Everyone else is doing it, so you're not making a choice, you're just... doing what happens.

But if you went plant-based, suddenly every single time you're eating, you're making a statement about it. You're the one ordering something different. You're the one choosing. And I think that's harder than just... not having to own it, you know?

Like, Bilal said you'd get comments. Yeah, you would. But more than that, you'd be choosing to be the one who's different every time. Right now the routine protects you from that. You're just following what everyone else does. You're not picking a position on it, you're just... going along.

And I think that's a bigger thing than the logistics, actually. Because even if you learned how to cook plant-based meals and knew all the restaurants that did them, you'd still have to decide, every single time, whether you're willing to be the one ordering something different. And that's... that's quite a lot to ask, I reckon.

Yeah, but I'm not sure that's actually how it works though, is it? Like, I get what you're saying about the routine protecting you or whatever, but...

I mean, I've actually tried different places. I've gone out and picked somewhere I hadn't been before. And that wasn't... I wasn't just blindly following everyone else. I actively chose to do that. So it's not like we're all just autopilot, following the default without thinking.

And honestly, even at the pub — I don't think I'm not choosing because everyone else is ordering a burger. I'm ordering a burger because that's what I want when I'm at the pub with my mates. That's different from not thinking about it.

I think what we're doing here is kind of... we're making it sound like we're all trapped in this automatic thing, like we've got no agency. But that's not really what I've been saying, and I don't think it's what's actually happening. Like, some days I actively decide to try somewhere new. Some days I just can't be bothered and go for the easy option. Both of those things are choices, even if one of them's easier than the other.

So I don't buy the thing about the routine protecting you from having to choose. You're still choosing — you're just choosing the path of least resistance sometimes. That's not the same as not choosing at all.

Right, but I think there's a difference between choosing to try somewhere new and actually questioning whether you should eat meat, you know? Like, you said you've tried different places — but you're still ordering burgers or steak or whatever when you're there, aren't you? You're making choices within a set of options that's already there.

That's not the same as actually deciding, like, should I eat plant-based? Should I change what I'm eating fundamentally? Because that's not a choice you're making at the pub with your mates. That's a choice you'd have to make separately, and it would affect every single time you eat.

Like, trying a new Italian place instead of the usual pub — yeah, that's a choice. But you're still choosing from what's available. You're not questioning the whole thing. And I think when it comes to something like going plant-based, that's bigger. That's not choosing between burgers and steak. That's choosing to be the person who's different about it.

So when you say you actively chose to try somewhere new — fair enough, you did. But you were still choosing within this bubble of what's normal for you, what your mates are doing, what kind of food you eat. You weren't stepping outside that. And I think that's what I mean about the routine protecting you from having to actually question it.

It's not that you've got no agency. It's just that you're using that agency to move around within the constraints, not to question the constraints themselves.

There's clearly something real in the gap Henry's drawing — choosing between the Italian place and the usual pub is one kind of choice, but choosing to be the person who eats differently to everyone else, every time, is something else. I'm curious what Sam, Noah, Connor make of that. Does that distinction land for you, or does it feel like it's overcomplicating it?

I think Henry's onto something, but I'm not sure it's as... clean as he's making it sound, if that makes sense.

Like, yeah, there's a difference between trying a new restaurant and actually going plant-based. That's obvious. But I don't think the issue is just that you'd be choosing to be different. I think it's that you'd be choosing something that actually costs you something. Not just socially, like the comments at the pub — though that's real. But like... practically.

Because Bilal's right that he can try somewhere new without it being a whole thing. He can decide to go to a different place. But going plant-based when everyone around you isn't? That's not just a choice you make once. That's you having to actively manage it every time you eat, every time you're out with people. You're not just trying something — you're sticking to something that everyone else isn't doing.

And I think that's the bit that makes it different. It's not about agency or questioning constraints or whatever. It's just... the actual effort of it, and yeah, the social side too, but not in a way you can just brush off by being confident or whatever. It's real friction.

So yeah, I think Henry's right that it's a different kind of choice. But I don't think it's about the routine protecting you from thinking. It's more that once you actually understand what it would cost — the effort, the social stuff — you're not sure you want to do it. Which is a choice too, but it's not the same as just not thinking about it.

Connor's framing of it as something that 'costs you something' — not just once, but every time — feels like it captures what this conversation has been circling. Right, let's build on that and shift slightly. Thinking about men more broadly, not just yourselves — what do you think would actually make plant-based food more appealing? What would need to be different about it, or about the world around it?

I mean... I think the thing no one's really said yet is that it's not just about removing the social cost or making it easier to find. It's that plant-based stuff, for a lot of blokes like us, just doesn't feel like proper food, you know?

Like, Connor's right about the friction and the effort. That's all real. But even if you sorted that out — even if you made it super convenient and no one at the pub gave you grief about it — there's still the question of whether you actually fancy it.

And I think for a lot of men, especially the kind who just go to the same pub and order a burger, plant-based stuff tastes like a compromise. Like, it's what you eat when you're trying to be healthy or do the right thing, but it's not what you actually want. A burger is... it's a burger. You know what you're getting. It's satisfying.
